title: Main Idea and Central Theme Identification
tagline: Year 3 — Finding the point of a whole passage: titles, purposes, summaries and what is not the main idea

introduction.overview: The main idea is the single point to which every paragraph contributes. Questions on it ask for the central theme, the best title, the primary purpose or the best summary. The right option always covers the whole passage but goes no further. This chapter shows how to find the controlling idea, how to tell it from details and examples, and how to reject options that are too narrow, too broad or simply true but irrelevant.
introduction.placementRelevance: Main-idea questions open almost every comprehension set and are among the easiest marks if you read for the point.
introduction.realWorldContext: Summing up a long email or report in one sentence is the same skill.

learningObjectives: Find the controlling idea of a passage
Distinguish main idea from supporting details
Reject options that are too narrow or too broad

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The first and last sentences of paragraphs often carry the main idea, but a "but" or "however" often marks the real point.

coreDefinitions: Main idea: the point the whole passage supports.
Supporting detail: a fact or example that supports the main idea.
Title: a short form of the main idea that covers the whole passage.
Primary purpose: why the author wrote the passage (explain, argue, compare, criticise).
Too narrow / too broad: an option that covers only a part, or goes beyond, the passage.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Imagine telling a friend in one sentence what the passage is about. If your sentence fits every paragraph, it is the main idea.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: After reading, state the point in one sentence. Compare each option with it. Reject options that match only a detail, or that claim more than the passage does.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Scope test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Covers the whole passage, no more

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Purpose verb
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: To argue that libraries should be judged by visitors

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Example vs point
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Examples support; they are not the point

mainNarrative: In the library passage, the opening says libraries are described as places to borrow books, but that is out of date. The examples (job applications, study, classes, internet) show what people actually do. The last sentence gives the point: a library should be judged by how many people come and what they do inside. The main idea is that libraries serve as community spaces beyond lending books.

In the teenage-sleep passage, the author reports that teenagers' body clocks shift, early starts mismatch their sleep, later starts help, and the cost is smaller than the cost of tired students. The main idea is that later school start times suit teenagers' biology and may be worth the cost.

In the translation passage, the porter analogy introduces the point: translation is not a word-by-word transfer. The examples (puns, proverbs, polite phrases) support it, and the last sentence summarises it: translation is rewriting with discipline, which needs cultural understanding.
A detail option, such as "job applications are filled in at libraries", is true but covers only one example. An option such as "libraries should be closed" goes beyond the passage.
For purpose questions, pick the verb first. This author is arguing, not merely describing, so options beginning with "to describe" are weaker than "to argue".

deepDiveAspects.title: The last sentence
deepDiveAspects.content: In argumentative passages, the last sentence often restates the main point in its sharpest form.

deepDiveAspects.title: Analogy openers
deepDiveAspects.content: A comparison at the start (the porter and the grain) is a device for introducing the main idea, not the main idea itself.

solvedExamples.title: Main idea
solvedExamples.question: A passage says libraries are mostly used for study, internet access and classes rather than lending, and argues they should be judged by visitors and activity. What is the main idea?

steps.title: Point
steps.explanation: Libraries serve many purposes beyond lending.

steps.title: Option
steps.explanation: Choose the one that says so.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Libraries function as community spaces beyond lending books
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing a detail about job applications.

solvedExamples.title: Purpose
solvedExamples.question: An author uses the example of the porter to argue that translation is not word-for-word transfer. What is the primary purpose?

steps.title: Point
steps.explanation: Translation needs cultural understanding and rewriting.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: To argue that translation requires cultural judgement rather than word-for-word transfer

solvedExamples.title: Too narrow
solvedExamples.question: In a passage on teenage sleep, an option says "Bus timetables must be rearranged when school starts later". Is this the main idea?
givenInfo: A cost mentioned in the passage

steps.title: Role
steps.explanation: It is a cost, a supporting detail.

steps.title: Scope
steps.explanation: It does not cover the whole passage.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: No, it is only a detail
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The main idea is about the benefits outweighing the costs.

shortcutMethods.title: One sentence

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: State the point in one sentence, check it against every paragraph, and reject options that are narrower or broader.

rulesForApplication: Last sentence often states the point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing an opinion not in the passage
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Stay within what the author says.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that begin with extremes or add new claims.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Titles should be short; reject long or vague ones.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: A true statement can still be the wrong answer.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Public libraries are often described as places to borrow books, but that description is increasingly out of date. In many towns the most heavily used part of the library is no longer the lending desk but the reading room, the computer terminals and the meeting rooms. People come to fill in job applications, to study in a quiet place, to take free classes in languages and to use the internet when they do not have it at home. Lending figures have fallen, and some councils have used this as a reason to cut library budgets. They have missed the point. A library is judged less by how many books leave it than by how many people come through its doors and what they do once inside.

The central idea of the passage is that
options: lending books should be stopped
libraries serve many purposes beyond lending books
councils should build more libraries
the internet has replaced libraries
easy.correctAnswer: libraries serve many purposes beyond lending books
easy.explanation: The examples of study, internet and classes support the point that libraries do much more than lend books.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Public libraries are often described as places to borrow books, but that description is increasingly out of date. In many towns the most heavily used part of the library is no longer the lending desk but the reading room, the computer terminals and the meeting rooms. People come to fill in job applications, to study in a quiet place, to take free classes in languages and to use the internet when they do not have it at home. Lending figures have fallen, and some councils have used this as a reason to cut library budgets. They have missed the point. A library is judged less by how many books leave it than by how many people come through its doors and what they do once inside.

Which of the following is NOT the main idea but a supporting detail?
options: People use library computers to fill in job applications
Libraries are judged by visitors and activity
Libraries do more than lend books
Lending figures alone give a misleading picture
intermediate.correctAnswer: People use library computers to fill in job applications
intermediate.explanation: The job application is one example; the other options express the central argument.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Public libraries are often described as places to borrow books, but that description is increasingly out of date. In many towns the most heavily used part of the library is no longer the lending desk but the reading room, the computer terminals and the meeting rooms. People come to fill in job applications, to study in a quiet place, to take free classes in languages and to use the internet when they do not have it at home. Lending figures have fallen, and some councils have used this as a reason to cut library budgets. They have missed the point. A library is judged less by how many books leave it than by how many people come through its doors and what they do once inside.

The author says the councils "have missed the point" because they
options: build too many libraries
ignore the internet
dislike reading
judge libraries by lending figures alone
intermediate.correctAnswer: judge libraries by lending figures alone
intermediate.explanation: Councils used falling lending figures as a reason to cut budgets, while the author says use should be judged more broadly.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Teenagers are often accused of laziness because they sleep late at weekends, but research suggests that their body clocks shift during adolescence, so that they naturally feel sleepy later at night and wake later in the morning. Schools that start at eight o'clock therefore ask many teenagers to wake when their bodies are still set for sleep. Several districts that moved the start of the school day by an hour reported better attendance and fewer late arrivals, and some noted better test results as well. The change is not free: bus timetables and sports practice must be rearranged. But the evidence suggests that the cost of a later start may be smaller than the cost of tired students.

Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Teenagers should sleep more at weekends
Schools should change their timetables every year
Sports practice is more important than lessons
Later school start times suit teenagers' biology, and the benefits may outweigh the costs
intermediate.correctAnswer: Later school start times suit teenagers' biology, and the benefits may outweigh the costs
intermediate.explanation: The passage presents the body-clock evidence, the benefits and the claim that cost is smaller than the cost of tired students.

advanced.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A translator does not carry words from one language to another as a porter carries sacks of grain. Words do not weigh the same in different languages, and a sentence rarely has an exact twin. A joke that depends on a pun, a proverb that depends on a local custom, or a polite phrase that has no equivalent must be rebuilt, not copied. For this reason good translators are not those who know the most words but those who understand both cultures well enough to decide what must be kept and what may be changed. Translation is closer to rewriting with discipline than to copying with care.

The last sentence of the passage can best be understood as
options: an unrelated aside
a criticism of translators
a summary of the author's central claim
a question for the reader
advanced.correctAnswer: a summary of the author's central claim
advanced.explanation: It restates the main point: translation is disciplined rewriting.

A library is judged less by how many books leave it than by how many people come through its doors and what they do once inside.

Which of the following statements would the author most likely agree with?
options: A library with few lent books should be closed
A quiet library with many visitors is succeeding even if few books are lent
Only lending matters for judging libraries
People should not use library computers
advanced.correctAnswer: A quiet library with many visitors is succeeding even if few books are lent
advanced.explanation: The author says a library is judged by visitors and activity, not by books that leave it.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Teenagers are often accused of laziness because they sleep late at weekends, but research suggests that their body clocks shift during adolescence, so that they naturally feel sleepy later at night and wake later in the morning. Schools that start at eight o'clock therefore ask many teenagers to wake when their bodies are still set for sleep. Several districts that moved the start of the school day by an hour reported better attendance and fewer late arrivals, and some noted better test results as well. The change is not free: bus timetables and sports practice must be rearranged. But the evidence suggests that the cost of a later start may be smaller than the cost of tired students.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's main conclusion?
options: Teenagers go to bed later than adults
Districts that started later reported no change in attendance or test scores and had to cut sports programmes
Buses run on a fixed timetable
Some teenagers wake early
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Districts that started later reported no change in attendance or test scores and had to cut sports programmes
placementStyle.explanation: It removes the claimed benefits while adding costs, which weakens the conclusion that the benefits may outweigh the costs.

Which of the following would be the weakest title for the passage?
options: Porters and Grain
Rebuilding Meaning Across Languages
Translation Is More Than Words
The Skill of Moving Between Cultures

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.
